metadata.title: Editorial research hypotheses and possible future investigations
metadata.scope: 32 unverified proposed hypotheses across 16 historical editorial method labels; no evidence-gap review has been conducted
metadata.source_note: The 16 labels came from a retired legacy regex taxonomy and are not the 12 official ISPOR topic groups. Contextual author-reported statements do not establish that a particular research gap exists.
metadata.coverage: 16 editorial legacy-method themes, 2 proposed hypotheses each; not a conference-level evidence assessment
metadata.claim_link_semantics: Illustrative contextual statements only; support versus contradiction versus irrelevance has not been independently assessed

themes.intro: How much of the clinical evidence available at launch can answer the actual EU assessment questions?

items.gap: Many scoped PICOs can lack a defensible comparative evidence pathway, even when an application includes pivotal clinical data.
items.direction: Audit each PICO against its available studies, comparator network, endpoints and maturity; report the proportion supported by direct, anchored indirect, unanchored or no comparison, and why.
items.decision: Quantifies which JCA questions can be answered and where additional evidence generation is needed.

items.gap: Effect-modifier choice and indirect comparison plans may be poorly aligned with the questions assessors evaluate.
items.direction: Compare pre-specified versus post-hoc adjustment sets using documented clinical justification, available aggregate covariates and sensitivity analyses; test how conclusions change.
items.decision: Separates avoidable analytical limitations from genuine evidence gaps.

themes.intro: Which AI-assisted HEOR tasks are reproducible and safe enough for decision-grade evidence?

items.gap: Benchmarking often lacks a shared definition of acceptable errors, gold-standard datasets and independently reproducible performance estimates.
items.direction: Construct externally annotated datasets for screening, extraction, PICO identification and model QA; report recall, precision, factual errors, time saved and disagreement resolution.
items.decision: Tests actual workflow reliability instead of assuming automation equals validity.

items.gap: Prospective evidence on how AI affects human reviewer workload, bias and correction costs remains limited.
items.direction: Run paired human versus human-plus-AI studies with blinded adjudication; record model version, prompt, human corrections and downstream impact of missed evidence.
items.decision: Shows when AI accelerates work without reducing decision quality.

themes.intro: How do model structure, uncertainty and distributional consequences affect reimbursement conclusions?

items.gap: Alternative plausible model structures can produce different long-term costs and QALYs, yet their contribution to uncertainty may be insufficiently isolated.
items.direction: Use prespecified structural scenarios, external validation, model averaging where justified and a transparent decomposition of parameter versus structural uncertainty.
items.decision: Identifies where the reimbursement conclusion depends on modelling choices.

items.gap: A positive population-average ICER may hide affordability, implementation or subgroup inequities.
items.direction: Link cost-effectiveness, budget impact, uptake constraints and distributional outcomes using consistent eligible populations and time horizons.
items.decision: Tests whether a cost-effective intervention can be implemented equitably within payer constraints.

themes.intro: When can observational evidence emulate the decision-relevant trial well enough for HTA?

items.gap: Treatment eligibility, time zero and outcome measurement are not always captured consistently across real-world datasets.
items.direction: Pre-register an explicit target-trial protocol and test sensitivity to treatment grace periods, outcome ascertainment and missing covariates across databases.
items.decision: Clarifies whether a real-world estimate answers the intended clinical question.

items.gap: Transporting a treatment effect from one healthcare system or registry to another may fail when important effect modifiers differ.
items.direction: Evaluate overlap, transport weights, subgroup heterogeneity and external calibration against independent datasets.
items.decision: Defines which payer population can reasonably use the evidence.

themes.intro: How robust are comparative effectiveness estimates to design choices and unmeasured confounding?

items.gap: Time-varying treatment and confounders can create selection or immortal-time bias if analysed as fixed baseline variables.
items.direction: Compare emulated dynamic treatment strategies, appropriate longitudinal weighting or g-methods, and simpler baseline analyses under a common estimand.
items.decision: Shows when treatment-effect estimates are driven by exposure timing instead of clinical differences.

items.gap: Residual confounding and treatment positivity problems are often difficult to quantify from routine data.
items.direction: Pre-specify overlap diagnostics, negative controls and quantitative bias analyses; report effect estimates under alternative target populations.
items.decision: Identifies when causal conclusions remain fragile despite good measured covariate balance.

themes.intro: What makes indirect comparisons credible when head-to-head trials are absent?

items.gap: The clinical justification for prognostic factors and treatment effect modifiers may not be reproducible, especially with limited aggregate data.
items.direction: Publish covariate-selection rationales and evaluate sensitivity to alternative adjustment sets, population overlap and effective sample size.
items.decision: Makes the direction and magnitude of adjustment bias visible.

items.gap: Sparse or disconnected treatment networks can make results highly dependent on assumptions about relative effects.
items.direction: Benchmark anchored and unanchored approaches in simulation scenarios with known treatment effects and realistic between-study heterogeneity.
items.decision: Separates statistical precision from identification of a credible treatment contrast.

themes.intro: Can multilevel network meta-regression be transported into economic models without changing the target estimand?

items.gap: Survival predicted at mean covariates may differ from survival marginalised across the target population, particularly under strong effect modification or nonlinear hazards.
items.direction: Compare conditional approximations with numerical marginalisation across realistic covariate distributions, correlation structures and follow-up horizons.
items.decision: Defines when an Excel approximation changes the economic decision.

items.gap: Computational shortcuts can obscure numerical integration error, baseline survival assumptions and uncertainty propagation.
items.direction: Benchmark Excel implementations against independently validated R or Stan models over PSA runs and complex survival functions, documenting runtime and numerical tolerances.
items.decision: Balances reproducibility and speed against bias in long-term predictions.

themes.intro: How credible are long-term survival predictions when follow-up is immature?

items.gap: Several distributions may fit observed data equally well yet imply materially different long-term mortality or cure behaviour.
items.direction: Compare extrapolations against external cohorts, clinical plausibility constraints and later data cuts; report decision sensitivity to tail assumptions.
items.decision: Shows how much of the ICER depends on unobserved survival.

items.gap: Treatment-effect waning and post-progression survival relationships may not be supported by the same evidence used to fit primary survival endpoints.
items.direction: Validate linked endpoint and treatment-duration assumptions using available patient-level information, independent data and structural stress tests.
items.decision: Prevents apparently precise model outputs from masking poorly identified long-term pathways.

themes.intro: When is borrowing external evidence helpful rather than misleading?

items.gap: The external data used to form informative priors may differ from the target study in prognosis, treatment pathways or endpoint definition.
items.direction: Assess prior-data conflict, commensurability and dynamic borrowing using prespecified sensitivity analyses and simulated operating characteristics.
items.decision: Avoids overconfident predictions when external populations are not exchangeable.

items.gap: Posterior results can be sensitive to priors without that dependence being clear to decision-makers.
items.direction: Report weak, sceptical and evidence-informed prior scenarios, posterior predictive checks and the resulting reimbursement decision probabilities.
items.decision: Makes the incremental influence of expert and external evidence transparent.

themes.intro: What is the actual effect of international price referencing on launches and access?

items.gap: Policy announcements and industry expectations do not establish whether MFN has caused delays, withdrawals or reduced access in European countries.
items.direction: Create a dated country-policy and launch panel; compare pre-policy and post-policy launch timing with credible controls and explicit alternative explanations.
items.decision: Distinguishes predicted manufacturer behaviour from observed consequences.

items.gap: Changes in list prices, confidential discounts and treated patient volumes may move in different directions.
items.direction: Model and, where data permit, estimate net expenditure, access volume and launch decisions jointly rather than using list prices alone.
items.decision: Identifies the price-access trade-off relevant to patients and payers.

themes.intro: What happens after a positive HTA or reimbursement decision?

items.gap: Approval or listing dates do not establish actual treatment initiation, geographic availability or continuity of therapy.
items.direction: Link regulatory, reimbursement, procurement and patient-level dispensing data to measure the interval from authorisation to real uptake.
items.decision: Distinguishes nominal coverage from effective access.

items.gap: International pricing strategies can shift availability between countries with different negotiating power and payment constraints.
items.direction: Examine launch sequence, confidential arrangements and patient access jointly across markets; adjust for regulatory and clinical-demand differences.
items.decision: Tests whether pricing strategies improve access overall or redistribute delays.

themes.intro: How can large and increasingly automated evidence reviews remain complete and auditable?

items.gap: AI-assisted screening and extraction studies do not always report enough performance information to estimate missed-study risk.
items.direction: Adopt explicit datasets, screening recall, precision, work saved, extraction agreement and human adjudication reports for every automated step.
items.decision: Allows assessors to quantify the completeness-efficiency trade-off.

items.gap: Changing search results and model versions can impair reproducibility and selective retrieval may affect indirect comparison networks.
items.direction: Publish versioned searches, deduplication rules, model prompts where appropriate, rejected-study logs and repeatable audit trails.
items.decision: Keeps downstream treatment comparisons traceable to the underlying study universe.

themes.intro: Can clinical evidence cover the populations, interventions, comparators and outcomes requested by HTA?

items.gap: One pivotal study can be relevant to several PICOs but provide no valid comparison for a subset of required comparators.
items.direction: Build machine-readable PICO-to-evidence matrices with explicit inclusion, exclusion and indirect-comparison feasibility reasons.
items.decision: Prevents an apparent study count from being confused with answerable assessment questions.

items.gap: PICO boundaries and outcome definitions may differ between regulatory trials and national decision needs.
items.direction: Map trial eligibility, endpoint timing and outcome definitions to decision populations and rerun analyses for material mismatches.
items.decision: Makes evidence applicability a testable rather than assumed property.

themes.intro: Is the treatment effect estimated actually the effect the clinical and payer decision requires?

items.gap: Rescue medication, switching, discontinuation and missing outcomes can alter the effect targeted during analysis, without transparent documentation.
items.direction: Write the intended estimand before analysis, record intercurrent-event strategies, and compare target versus realised estimands in a structured table.
items.decision: Avoids interpreting an effect for one treatment strategy as evidence for another.

items.gap: Trial estimands and target-trial emulations may differ in follow-up, eligibility and adherence handling.
items.direction: Develop matched protocol diagrams and benchmark treatment-policy, hypothetical and per-protocol effects using common endpoint definitions.
items.decision: Improves transfer of clinical effectiveness evidence into HTA.

themes.intro: Do patient-reported measures capture the benefit and burden relevant to different populations?

items.gap: Generic utility measures may be insensitive to short-lived symptoms, treatment burden or disease-specific changes in patient experience.
items.direction: Validate responsiveness and mapping against condition-specific instruments, then test how the choice of instrument changes QALYs.
items.decision: Shows which aspects of patient benefit are omitted in an economic model.

items.gap: Missing patient-reported data may be associated with worsening health, treatment discontinuation or unequal participation.
items.direction: Compare missing-data mechanisms and joint or pattern-mixture sensitivity analyses, including language and subgroup measurement equivalence.
items.decision: Tests whether apparent quality-of-life gains depend on who remains observed.

themes.intro: How does real-world implementation change the value of devices compared with trial conditions?

items.gap: Device performance, complication rates and costs may depend on operator experience, hospital volume and training, which are rarely constant across sites.
items.direction: Evaluate centre-level learning curves and volume-outcome relationships; incorporate dynamic adoption and capacity constraints into cost-effectiveness models.
items.decision: Explains why effectiveness and affordability can differ between trial centres and ordinary hospitals.

items.gap: Rapid product iteration can outpace clinical trials and create uncertainty about transferring evidence between device versions.
items.direction: Use post-market registries and version-specific reassessments with clear linkage between the assessed device and observed outcomes.
items.decision: Avoids using historical evidence for a materially changed technology without validation.
